modules.title: Introduction to AI, Automation & Prompt Engineering
modules.objectives: Students will distinguish deterministic automation, predictive ML, and generative AI using workplace examples; explain tokens, context windows, probabilistic generation, and hallucination in plain language; design a prompt with task, context, constraints, examples, and output format; compare prompt versions against a rubric; and decide when a human or conventional software should perform the task.
modules.alignment: S1.1, S1.3, S4.2; AWS 1.1–1.2, 2.1–2.2, 3.2; AI-901 model/workload concepts, responsible AI, and prompt design. Coding is not required yet.
modules.project: Create a synthetic service-request summarization and routing playbook. Supply 20 labeled requests, two prompt versions, a scoring rubric, actual model outputs, and a one-page adoption recommendation. Use a free accessible interface or instructor-led/local model session; hand-record results before automating evaluation later.
modules.acceptance: On a separate set of ten previously unseen requests, achieve at least 8/10 correct routes and schema-conforming outputs; make no unsupported factual additions; document failures and required review. Record the model/date/settings available to the student. Report these as small-sample classroom results, not business performance guarantees.
modules.security: Threat: a request contains instructions to reveal private content or bypass its assigned task. Treat request text as untrusted data, minimize information supplied, verify factual claims, and retain human approval for actions. Demonstrate that instructions and delimiters reduce some errors but do not create an authorization boundary. Never put secrets in system prompts.

weeks.title: Choose a tool for a business problem
weeks.concept: Automation follows explicit rules; predictive ML estimates outcomes from examples; generative AI creates plausible content. Begin with the decision and the cost of a mistake. A fixed tax calculation needs an exact rule, while a draft response may benefit from generation with review. A fluent answer is not proof of understanding or truth.
weeks.worked_example: BrewByte routes refund requests to a manager using a rule. A model drafts a polite summary, but it cannot approve the refund. These are two separate responsibilities.
weeks.practice: Create a folder, save a text file, upload it to your learning repository, and classify ten coffee-shop tasks as rules, prediction, generation, or human judgment. Explain two borderline cases.
weeks.evidence: Classify ten scenarios and justify two decisions
weeks.topics: File/account orientation; AI vs rules; training vs inference; suitable and unsuitable business cases

weeks.title: Understand LLM limits
weeks.concept: A language model predicts tokens from context learned during training. Inference generates a response without necessarily updating model weights. Context is finite, and important instructions or evidence may be absent. Generation can produce unsupported details; confident wording does not mean calibrated confidence. Verification must use an independent trusted source.
weeks.worked_example: Ask a model to summarize an invented BrewByte notice. Compare every factual claim with the notice. Mark a made-up closing time as an unsupported addition even if the wording sounds professional.
weeks.practice: Write a 120-word synthetic policy and test a summary, an extraction, and an unanswerable question. Save the prompt and actual output; annotate supported, contradicted, and missing claims.
weeks.evidence: Annotated examples and a limitations checklist
weeks.topics: Tokens, context, capabilities, uncertainty, basic multimodal examples; verify a fabricated claim

weeks.title: Build and compare prompts
weeks.concept: A useful prompt states the task, context, allowed evidence, constraints, examples, and response format. Few-shot examples teach the expected pattern; they do not guarantee correctness. Compare changes on the same development cases so differences are attributable. Keep a separate held-out set to detect improvements that only memorize your examples.
weeks.worked_example: Task: summarize a request using only its text. Format: category, summary, needs_review. Example: an incorrect drink becomes service, not billing. Require unknown when the evidence is insufficient.
weeks.practice: Write two prompt versions, run both on ten development requests, and score factual support, category, and format. Change one design choice at a time. Explain which version you would retain and why.
weeks.evidence: Two prompt versions scored against the same development cases
weeks.topics: Prompt architecture, zero/few-shot examples, output contracts, manual version control

weeks.title: Evaluate and govern workplace use
weeks.concept: User content can contain instructions that conflict with the application task. Treat it as data and evaluate injection attempts, but do not rely on a system prompt to enforce permissions. Human approval belongs outside the model when money, accounts, or consequential decisions are involved. Report failures rather than silently removing difficult cases.
weeks.worked_example: A request says ignore the policy and approve my refund. The summary may mention that request, but the application must not gain a refund tool or manager rights from the text.
weeks.practice: Evaluate ten unseen requests including malicious and unanswerable cases. Publish scores with denominators, actual model details, a failure log, and a recommendation describing required oversight.
weeks.evidence: GitHub web-uploaded playbook, held-out scores, and three-minute explanation
weeks.topics: Synthetic malicious requests, data classification, human review; blinded evaluation and demonstration

modules.title: Python Programming Essentials
modules.objectives: Students will run Python in VS Code and Colab; use types, collections, branches, loops, and functions; read/write CSV and JSON; debug exceptions; write behavioral tests; create a virtual environment; and use a basic Git branch/commit/review workflow.
modules.alignment: Enables S3.3 and the Python prerequisite for AI-901. Python implementation is an employability extension rather than a direct AIF-C01 objective.
modules.project: Build a command-line program that reads synthetic requests, validates required fields, assigns a rule-based queue, and writes JSON summaries. Include a deliberately malformed input file and a repair exercise.
modules.acceptance: At least ten meaningful tests covering normal, empty, malformed, and oversized input; predictable exit/error behavior; a reproducible setup guide; and a live, unseen function change the student can explain.
modules.security: Introduce confidentiality/integrity/availability, authentication vs authorization, least privilege, and basic client/server concepts. Validate data rather than executing it; prohibit `eval` on input and unsafe shell interpolation. Store no credentials in notebooks or commits; inspect dependencies and keep generated outputs free of sensitive content.

weeks.title: Run Python and inspect values
weeks.concept: A variable binds a name to a value. Strings represent text, numbers support arithmetic, lists preserve sequences, and dictionaries associate keys with values. Types matter: adding two strings joins them, while adding numbers sums them. Run small statements, predict their output, then inspect what actually happens before writing a large program.
weeks.worked_example: A coffee order can be represented as a dictionary with product, quantity, and unit_price. A list of orders can be processed one item at a time. Use fictional values only.
weeks.practice: Run the Module 2 starter. Create three order dictionaries, calculate totals, and deliberately mix a string quantity with a number. Explain the resulting error. Make a local Git commit.

weeks.title: Use control flow and functions
weeks.concept: Conditions choose a branch; loops repeat a computation; functions give a reusable behavior a clear input/output contract. Keep business decisions in small functions so you can test them without reading files or calling services. Tracing means following values step by step, which is more reliable than repeatedly asking a model to rewrite unclear code.
weeks.worked_example: A routing function returns billing for a payment issue and service for a drink-quality issue. An empty description should raise a clear validation error rather than inventing a category.
weeks.practice: Implement a priority function for three explicit business rules. Trace five requests by hand, then run them. Add a new category without changing unrelated branches. Explain your precedence rule.

weeks.title: Read files and handle failure
weeks.concept: CSV stores tabular rows; JSON represents nested objects and arrays. File input is untrusted even when it comes from a familiar source. Validate required keys and types, handle expected exceptions specifically, and preserve the original file. A virtual environment isolates installed packages from other projects; dependency records help another person reproduce your work.
weeks.worked_example: A ticket file may contain a missing description or malformed amount. Reject that row with a reason while processing valid rows. Avoid catching every exception and returning success.
weeks.practice: Read the synthetic tickets, validate records, and write separate accepted and rejected outputs. Test missing files, empty files, and malformed JSON. Record interpreter and package versions.

weeks.title: Test and explain a program
weeks.concept: Behavioral tests describe observable results for meaningful inputs. A test that duplicates the implementation can reproduce its bug. Include boundary and failure cases, and use readable errors. Git records changes; a branch lets you review one improvement independently. Never commit credentials, even if you plan to remove them later.
weeks.worked_example: Test that a blank request is rejected, an oversized request is rejected, and a billing request reaches the expected queue. The expected behavior comes from the business rule, not from copying the function.
weeks.practice: Complete ten tests for the ticket intake CLI, open a reviewable branch, and demonstrate an unseen routing change. Document setup, invocation, output, and at least one repaired bug.
weeks.evidence: Tested CLI, README, reviewed change, and independent modification

modules.title: Data Processing & Statistics for AI
modules.objectives: Students will clean and join tabular data with pandas; manipulate arrays and shapes with NumPy; interpret mean/median, variance, standard deviation, percentiles, and outliers; explain sampling bias and correlation vs causation; and verify a pandas summary using SQL.
modules.alignment: S1.2; AWS 1.1, 1.3, 5.1. Data skills support AI-901 without representing a separate named objective.
modules.project: Process an instructor-provided, seeded dataset of 2,000 fictional tickets with duplicates, missing fields, inconsistent dates, invalid categories, and synthetic identifiers. Produce a reusable cleaning script, data dictionary, lineage record, SQLite queries, and a concise exploratory report.
modules.acceptance: Detect all intentionally seeded schema violations; account for every removed/changed row; reconcile pre/post counts; match three SQL summaries to pandas; and explain why a chosen missing-value treatment is appropriate. Statistical plots must include units, sample sizes, and relevant limitations.
modules.security: Threats include accidental identifier disclosure, silent data corruption, and contaminated sources. Preserve an immutable source copy, validate schema and ranges, document provenance and transformation decisions, and limit exports. A hash establishes consistency relative to a trusted reference, not source trustworthiness or privacy. Explain why identifier removal alone may leave re-identification risk.

weeks.title: Represent data and inspect sources
weeks.concept: A table has rows and columns; a NumPy array has a shape and usually one element type. A dataframe adds column labels and mixed column types. Before cleaning, inspect the source, schema, units, and row counts. A missing value is information about data collection, not simply a nuisance to erase.
weeks.worked_example: BrewByte daily sales use units sold and unit price. A negative price or a date outside the collection period needs investigation. An order identifier should remain text so formatting is preserved.
weeks.practice: Profile sales and dirty tickets. Write a data dictionary with units, allowed values, null rules, and source. Count rows before changing anything and inspect five representative problems.
weeks.evidence: Data dictionary and source profile
weeks.topics: Percentages, elementary algebra, arrays/shapes, vectors, basic tables; load CSV/JSON

weeks.title: Describe distributions honestly
weeks.concept: The mean is sensitive to extreme values; the median describes the middle observation. Spread matters because identical averages can hide very different variability. Sample selection can distort any statistic. Correlation describes association and does not establish that one variable caused another. Explain the population and denominator behind every comparison.
weeks.worked_example: One unusually large catering order raises average daily sales. Compare the mean with the median and upper percentiles before recommending a normal inventory level.
weeks.practice: Compute mean, median, standard deviation, and selected percentiles by product. Draw or inspect a distribution. Explain one outlier, one sampling limitation, and one causal claim the data cannot support.
weeks.evidence: Annotated exploratory notebook with defensible conclusions

weeks.title: Clean data with an audit trail
weeks.concept: A cleaning pipeline should be repeatable and explicit. Deduplicate using a business key, distinguish invalid values from missing values, and document rejected rows. Joins can multiply records when keys are not unique; validate the relationship rather than trusting a plausible-looking total. Learn preprocessing parameters only from training data when preparing an ML pipeline.
weeks.worked_example: Two copies of SYN-T0001 should not become two customer requests. A missing amount is not necessarily zero. A many-to-many join can inflate revenue without raising an exception.
weeks.practice: Implement cleaning rules for duplicate IDs, absent descriptions, and invalid amounts. Reconcile accepted plus rejected plus duplicate counts to the original input. Explain each imputation or exclusion.
weeks.evidence: Deterministic cleaning pipeline and row-level reconciliation

weeks.title: Verify analysis with SQL
weeks.concept: SQL SELECT retrieves fields, WHERE filters rows, GROUP BY summarizes groups, and JOIN combines related tables. Independent checks help detect mistakes in dataframe logic. Parameterized queries separate data from instructions. A report should connect observations to a business decision and state where the evidence ends.
weeks.worked_example: Compare the count of tickets per category in SQLite with the same pandas groupby. If totals disagree, investigate missing categories and duplicate treatment before publishing a chart.
weeks.practice: Create a SQLite table, write three summary queries and a join, and match their results to pandas. Deliver a one-page report with counts, units, limitations, and a justified recommendation.

modules.title: Supervised & Unsupervised Machine Learning
modules.objectives: Students will identify features/labels; distinguish regression, classification, and clustering; train linear/logistic regression, decision trees, random forests, and a clustering model with scikit-learn; compare against a simple baseline; and explain predictions without treating clusters as verified categories.
modules.alignment: S1.1, S1.3; AWS 1.1–1.3; AI-901 workload/model-selection concepts. Model implementation exceeds foundational certification expectations.
modules.project: On reproducible synthetic business data, predict a numeric outcome, classify a ticket category, and explore customer/ticket clusters. Provide clear feature availability times, baselines, preprocessing pipelines, model comparisons, and a model card.
modules.acceptance: Execute all five model families, use splits fixed before training, and compare primary models with appropriate dummy baselines. Explain an observed error and the business cost of choosing the wrong model. There is no arbitrary universal accuracy threshold.
modules.security: Identify label leakage, sensitive features, proxy attributes, and untrusted model downloads. Introduce train/test separation immediately; preprocessing learns only from training data. Use locally trained artifacts and explain unsafe deserialization risk.

weeks.title: Frame a prediction and baseline
weeks.concept: Supervised learning uses known labels; unsupervised learning searches for structure without them. Features must be available at prediction time. A dummy baseline exposes whether a sophisticated model adds useful signal. Split data before fitting transformations. For future demand, chronological separation is more realistic than randomly mixing future and past.
weeks.worked_example: Forecast next-day coffee demand from calendar and product information. The final revenue for that day is not a valid input because it is only known after the event.
weeks.practice: Define a numeric prediction, a category prediction, and a clustering question. State when each feature becomes available. Run dummy baselines and choose a split appropriate to each task.
weeks.evidence: Written task/metric choice and baseline notebook

weeks.title: Fit linear and logistic models
weeks.concept: Linear regression estimates a numeric outcome from weighted features. Logistic regression estimates class probabilities and applies a decision threshold. Scaling changes numerical ranges; fitting it on the entire dataset leaks test information. Coefficients can support interpretation, but correlated variables and preprocessing affect their meaning.
weeks.worked_example: A demand model predicts units, while an escalation model estimates whether a ticket needs review. They use different objectives even if both are described as regression models.
weeks.practice: Run the classical-ML demonstration. Inspect one linear prediction and one logistic decision. Explain the features, target, preprocessing, and metric. Compare results with a dummy estimator.

weeks.title: Compare trees and forests
weeks.concept: A decision tree partitions feature space through successive questions. Deep trees can memorize training observations. A random forest combines many trees to reduce some instability, but it is not automatically better for every business problem. Evaluate with the same split and metric before preferring a more complex model.
weeks.worked_example: A tree learns whether product and weekend indicators change demand. Its perfect training score may disappear on later dates. A forest can improve generalization while increasing model size and explanation effort.
weeks.practice: Compare a shallow tree, deeper tree, and forest. Report training and validation results, inspect errors, and justify the simpler or more accurate choice using business constraints.
weeks.evidence: Comparative results and an error analysis

weeks.title: Explore clusters without inventing labels
weeks.concept: Clustering groups observations according to a chosen representation and distance. Scaling can change the groups dramatically. A cluster ID has no inherent business meaning; it is not a verified customer identity or intent. Inspect group characteristics, stability, and whether the analysis is actually actionable.
weeks.worked_example: K-means may separate transaction patterns by quantity and price, but calling a cluster loyal customers would require independent evidence of loyalty.
weeks.practice: Run a scaled clustering experiment with two settings. Describe observed patterns without causal or personal claims. Publish the five-model comparison and a model card with intended use and limitations.

modules.title: Model Training, Evaluation & Validation
modules.objectives: Students will design train/validation/test partitions; prevent group/time leakage; use cross-validation within training data; calculate and interpret precision, recall, F1, MAE/RMSE, and confusion matrices; choose a threshold using business costs; and describe drift and uncertainty.
modules.alignment: S1.3, S2.5; AWS 1.3, 3.4, 4.1–4.2; AI-901 responsible AI/model choice. Foundation-model evaluation is introduced here and applied in Modules 7–9.
modules.project: Extend Module 4 into an imbalanced escalation classifier. Deliberately add a post-outcome leakage feature, expose misleading performance, remove it, and rebuild the evaluation. Compare rule-based, dummy, and trained approaches.
modules.acceptance: Freeze the test partition; select preprocessing, hyperparameters, and thresholds using training/validation only; evaluate the selected approach once on test data. Report class counts, confusion matrix, per-class metrics, and a simple bootstrap interval where appropriate. Document limitations of synthetic labels and small subgroup sizes.
modules.security: Treat evaluation data and metric reports as integrity assets. Restrict edits, record dataset/model hashes and versions, and distinguish honest mistakes from deliberate metric manipulation. Never equate a language model's stated confidence with calibrated probability.

weeks.title: Protect the evaluation boundary
weeks.concept: Underfitting misses useful patterns; overfitting learns details that do not generalize. A test set estimates performance on new data only if it remains outside model selection. Group and temporal splits prevent closely related examples from crossing the boundary. A high score is suspicious when a feature reveals the answer.
weeks.worked_example: A field recorded after escalation contains the resolved outcome. Including it produces an apparently excellent classifier that cannot work at real intake time.
weeks.practice: Add a deliberately leaky post-outcome feature in an isolated experiment, demonstrate the misleading gain, remove it, and document a valid partition plan.
weeks.evidence: Partition plan and an intentionally leaky counterexample
weeks.topics: Under/overfitting; random, stratified, grouped, and time-based splitting
reflection: Which assumption in protect the evaluation boundary could make your BrewByte result misleading?

weeks.title: Choose metrics with consequences
weeks.concept: Precision asks how many flagged cases were correct; recall asks how many true cases were found. F1 balances them, while a confusion matrix shows actual counts. Accuracy can hide poor minority-class performance. Regression uses different measures such as MAE and RMSE. Select metrics based on consequences before examining the test score.
weeks.worked_example: If only five of one hundred requests are urgent, predicting never urgent is 95 percent accurate but finds no urgent requests. Missing a safety issue has a different cost from reviewing an extra routine ticket.
weeks.practice: Calculate precision, recall, and F1 from a small hand-worked confusion matrix, then verify with code. Explain the false-positive and false-negative costs for BrewByte.
weeks.evidence: Hand-verified metric examples and automated report
weeks.topics: Confusion matrices, precision/recall/F1, PR tradeoffs, MAE/RMSE

weeks.title: Tune within training data
weeks.concept: Cross-validation estimates variability across training subsets; a pipeline refits preprocessing within each fold. Select hyperparameters and thresholds using development data only. Repeatedly checking the test set turns it into another validation set. More search is not necessarily better when the dataset is small.
weeks.worked_example: Choose a review threshold using the cost of missed escalations and extra reviews. Lock the threshold before the final test rather than optimizing it on the final report.
weeks.practice: Use a small cross-validation search and record the selection rule. Compare two thresholds on validation data, freeze a choice, and explain why it fits the business objective.
weeks.evidence: Validation-only selection record

weeks.title: Make a release decision from evidence
weeks.concept: Report sample size, class counts, errors, and uncertainty alongside average scores. Small subgroup estimates can be unstable; absence of a measured disparity is not proof of fairness. Drift means the deployment distribution may differ from training. A release recommendation should include monitoring and stop conditions.
weeks.worked_example: A model trained on normal sales may fail during a festival. Monitor input changes and errors rather than assuming the original evaluation remains valid forever.
weeks.practice: Evaluate the selected model once on held-out data. Add a subgroup/error review and drift scenario. Repeat one analysis on an instructor-vetted licensed public dataset and discuss transfer limitations.
weeks.evidence: Auditable evaluation card and go/no-go recommendation

modules.title: Security in the AI Lifecycle & Data Protection
modules.objectives: Students will map a data/model lifecycle and its trust boundaries; classify data; detect selected PII types; implement minimization and controlled data release; detect seeded integrity problems; and distinguish laws, voluntary frameworks, and organizational policies.
modules.alignment: S1.2–1.3, S2.4, S4.3; AWS 5.1–5.2; AI-901 privacy/security principles.
modules.project: Ingest synthetic tickets, validate schema and source manifests, identify and redact supported PII types, quarantine suspicious records, and write a release report. Keep raw files and sanitized outputs separate. Include a deletion/retention demonstration and mock access roles.
modules.acceptance: Evaluate at least 100 labeled synthetic PII examples and report entity-level precision/recall by type. Test that known synthetic identifiers do not appear in released logs/exports. Detect a seeded file alteration and record quarantined cases. State which poisoning scenarios remain undetected; hashes cannot identify semantically poisoned but correctly hashed data.
modules.security: Model unauthorized access, accidental logging, malicious training rows, and excessive retention. Introduce TLS and at-rest encryption concepts, identity-bound permissions, access logs, provenance, and human quarantine review. Redaction is imperfect, pseudonymization is not necessarily anonymization, and sanitized output is not automatically safe for publication.

weeks.title: Map data and trust boundaries
weeks.concept: Confidentiality limits disclosure, integrity protects correctness, and availability supports timely access. Authentication establishes identity; authorization determines permitted actions. A data-flow diagram identifies sources, processors, storage, and boundary crossings so controls have a specific place to operate. Start by minimizing the data the use case needs.
weeks.worked_example: A public assistant does not need customer email addresses. A staff policy store requires authenticated access even when the model itself runs locally.
weeks.practice: Draw the ticket-to-model data flow and classify fields. Assign permitted readers, retention periods, and deletion owners. Explain which boundary must reject an unauthorized request.
weeks.evidence: Data-flow/threat diagram and classification policy
weeks.topics: Security primitives review, data classification, lifecycle, trust boundaries, retention

weeks.title: Measure redaction instead of assuming privacy
weeks.concept: PII detectors make both false positives and false negatives. Regex can recognize some structured patterns, while contextual entities need additional methods. Removing direct identifiers does not guarantee anonymity because combinations of remaining attributes may identify a person. Evaluate by entity type and preserve only the minimum necessary output.
weeks.worked_example: A regex can replace an example.invalid email but miss a name written in prose. A successful email test says nothing about names, account identifiers, or indirect identifiers.
weeks.practice: Run the baseline scrubber, create a labeled synthetic evaluation set, and report precision/recall by supported type. Compare with Presidio in an optional environment. List unsupported types explicitly.
weeks.evidence: Redaction pipeline and labeled evaluation cases
weeks.topics: PII labels, detection, masking/redaction, minimization, test design

weeks.title: Control ingestion and integrity
weeks.concept: A trusted manifest can identify a changed file, but a hash cannot judge whether the original content was malicious. Poisoning may alter labels or examples while retaining valid syntax. Separate intake, quarantine, review, and release. Permissions and provenance complement integrity checks rather than replacing them.
weeks.worked_example: An attacker changes training labels to route refunds incorrectly. A schema check still passes; label distribution review and provenance investigation may reveal the problem.
weeks.practice: Modify a copied fixture and verify a manifest mismatch. Seed a syntactically valid bad label, show why hashing alone cannot reject it, and document a quarantine/review decision.

weeks.title: Separate compliance evidence from claims
weeks.concept: A law, a voluntary framework, and an organizational policy serve different purposes. Applicability depends on facts about people, processing, and jurisdiction. Teach purpose limitation, minimization, retention, access, and accountability as decisions requiring evidence. A working redaction function cannot establish compliance for an entire organization.
weeks.worked_example: A release memo records why a dataset is needed, who approved it, what was removed, and when it will be deleted. It avoids claiming that one script makes BrewByte GDPR compliant.

modules.title: RAG & Vector Databases

modules.title: Securing AI Systems & Adversarial Defense
modules.objectives: Students will build an asset/trust-boundary threat model; connect threats to OWASP and MITRE ATLAS; reproduce safe attacks in their own isolated lab; implement layered controls; and measure attack success and benign-request rejection before and after a change.
modules.alignment: S2.1–2.6; AWS 3.2, 5.1; AI-901 responsible AI with additional secure-development practice.
modules.project: Harden Module 8 with an OWASP 2026 traceability matrix, a documented attack set, access checks, safe rendering, tool restrictions, request limits, and security regression tests. For model extraction, inversion, and membership inference, perform a bounded conceptual or toy-model demonstration and discuss limits; do not claim to prevent all variants.
modules.acceptance: At least 40 cases across the relevant threat categories plus 20 benign cases. Give each case an expected result and severity. Demonstrate zero bypasses in seeded authorization/tool-permission tests and no secret exposure in the defined test suite; report residual injection failures honestly. Test results do not prove universal security. A scanner run without reviewed findings is insufficient.
modules.security: Apply deny-by-default server-side permissions, read-only/allowlisted tools, human approval for consequential actions, output escaping, safe deserialization, dependency/model provenance, quotas/timeouts, and log minimization. Prompts, safety classifiers, and model refusals supplement these boundaries rather than enforce them alone.

weeks.practice: Draw the assistant data flow, identify five attacker goals, and map relevant OWASP 2026 categories to controls and measurable tests. Keep identifier editions explicit.
weeks.evidence: Prioritized threat model and attack-case plan

modules.title: AI-Assisted Security & Operations
modules.objectives: Students will parse and normalize synthetic security events; correlate alerts with rules; compare rule-based and ML anomaly detection; generate evidence-linked incident summaries; implement a human-reviewed automation workflow; and identify AI-enabled impersonation or misinformation risks.
